Part-Time Hourly Pay to Annual Salary: The Formula, Paid Weeks, and Pro-Rata Math

Direct AnswerPart-time hourly pay to annual salary uses rate × hours × paid weeks. $22 an hour at 24 hours a week is $27,456 a year gross, $24,220.02 after federal tax.

Gross pay estimates
By Saahil•Published November 5, 2026•13 min read•Calculation Guides
A closer look

In this guide

The Short Answer: $27,456 a YearThe Formula: Rate × Hours × Paid Weeks$22 an Hour at Every Part-Time SchedulePaid Weeks vs Unpaid Weeks: The $2,112 DifferenceWhen Your Hours Change Every WeekWhat Lands in Your Bank Each MonthPro-Rata Salary: Reading a Salary Offer as a Part-TimerOvertime and Benefits: Two Part-Time TrapsAfter Taxes at Part-Time Hours (Federal Only)Nearby Rates at 24 Hours a WeekTwo Part-Time Jobs, One Annual TotalHow to Use the CalculatorLimitationsFrequently Asked QuestionsKey Takeaways & Action Plan

Use your actual work schedule for a more useful estimate.

Quick Answer

Part-time hourly pay turns into an annual salary with one formula: hourly rate × hours per week × paid weeks. At $22 an hour, 24 hours a week, and 52 paid weeks, that is $27,456 a year gross, or $528 a week, $1,056 biweekly, and $2,288 a month on average. After federal tax alone, a single filer keeps $24,220.02, or $2,018.34 a month.

The Short Answer: $27,456 a Year

At $22 an hour and 24 hours a week, part-time annual salary is $27,456 gross: $528 a week, $1,056 every two weeks, $1,144 semi-monthly, and $2,288 a month on average, before taxes. After federal income tax and FICA alone, a single filer on the 2026 standard deduction keeps $24,220.02, or $2,018.34 a month. That is 88.2% of gross pay, the highest keep-rate in this guide’s ladder, because so little of the income reaches the 12% bracket.

That headline is only as good as its three inputs, and part-time schedules are where all three go wrong. The rate is usually quoted right. The hours are usually guessed (a “roughly 25-hour” week that is really 22). And the paid weeks are usually assumed to be 52, when an hourly worker is paid for far fewer. This guide prices each input on its own: the hours ladder, the paid-weeks gap, variable hours, what actually lands each month, pro-rata salary offers, and the overtime and benefits traps. That way you can rebuild the figure on your own schedule instead of trusting someone else’s headline. Our hourly-to-annual conversion guide covers the full-time version of the same formula.

The Formula: Rate × Hours × Paid Weeks

Every conversion in this guide uses the same three inputs. Get those right and the rest is simple arithmetic:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Weekly gross$22 × 24 hours$528.00 per week
Step 2 — Annual gross$528 × 52 paid weeks$27,456.00
Step 3 — Biweekly$528 × 2 weeks$1,056.00
Step 4 — Semi-monthly$27,456 ÷ 24 paychecks$1,144.00
Step 5 — Monthly average$27,456 ÷ 12 months$2,288.00
Step 6 — Federal-only take-home$27,456 − $1,135.60 federal − $2,100.38 FICA$24,220.02

Three definitions matter. Hours per week means the hours you are paid for, not the hours you are scheduled in a good week, so use an average (see the variable-hours section). Paid weeks means the weeks your paycheck actually covers: a salaried part-timer on a pro-rata salary is paid 52 weeks, while an hourly part-timer who is unpaid over a shutdown or a holiday stretch is not. Annual salary here means gross pay before any tax or deduction, the same convention as every wage guide on this site.

Two shortcuts are worth dropping. The first is the 2,080-hour shortcut: multiplying any rate by 2,080 assumes a 40-hour week, so it overstates a 24-hour schedule by $17,600. It would claim $45,760 for this $22 rate, which is the full-time figure, not the part-time one. The second is the “times 4 weeks” month: $528 × 4 = $2,112 understates the true $2,288 monthly average by $176, because a month averages 4.33 weeks, not 4. Both mistakes come from borrowing a full-time convention for a part-time schedule.

$22 an Hour at Every Part-Time Schedule

The rate never changes in this table, only the hours do. That is exactly why two $22-an-hour offers can be worth very different years. Take-home is federal-only for a single filer under 2026 rules (standard deduction $16,100; FICA 7.65%):

Weekly hoursAnnual grossFederal-only take-homeTake-home per monthWatch out
12 (one-and-a-half days)$13,728.00$12,677.81$1,056.48Below the standard deduction — $0 federal income tax
16$18,304.00$16,683.34$1,390.28Still entirely in the 10% bracket
20 (half-time)$22,880.00$20,451.68$1,704.31The classic half-time line
24 (this guide’s anchor)$27,456.00$24,220.02$2,018.3488.2% kept — the bracket effect at its strongest
28$32,032.00$27,917.71$2,326.48Crosses into the 12% bracket
30 (ACA benefits line)$34,320.00$29,756.12$2,479.68See the benefits trap below
32$36,608.00$31,594.53$2,632.88Four 8-hour days
35$40,040.00$34,352.14$2,862.68Five 7-hour days — near-full-time pay, part-time label

Two things are worth noticing. First, the keep-rate falls as hours rise: 92.3% at 12 hours (no federal income tax at all, only FICA), 88.2% at 24 hours, 86.7% at 30 hours. That is because each extra hour is taxed at the marginal rate, while the earlier hours were taxed at lower ones. Second, the jump from 24 to 30 hours is worth $6,864 gross and $5,536.10 of take-home, which is more than a $1 raise at 24 hours would ever deliver. At part-time levels, hours move the year more than the rate does.

Paid Weeks vs Unpaid Weeks: The $2,112 Difference

Paid weeks are the input part-time workers get wrong most often, because job posts quote a rate and a schedule but rarely say which weeks are paid. Same rate, same 24-hour week, three different years:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — 52 paid weeks$528 × 52$27,456.00 gross / $24,220.02 take-home
Step 2 — 50 paid weeks (2 unpaid)$528 × 50$26,400.00 gross / $23,350.40 take-home
Step 3 — 48 paid weeks (4 unpaid)$528 × 48$25,344.00 gross / $22,480.78 take-home
Step 4 — Cost of 4 unpaid weeks$27,456 − $25,344$2,112.00 gross / $1,739.24 take-home

That cuts both ways. A salaried pro-rata offer keeps paying through a shutdown week; an hourly offer does not, and the $2,112 gap is exactly the price of that difference for this schedule. Before you accept, ask one question and get the answer in writing: “Which weeks of the year am I paid for?” If the answer is “all 52,” the headline holds. If it is “48, plus unpaid holidays,” price the offer at $25,344, not $27,456, and compare it against other offers on the same paid-week basis. Our hourly-versus-salary comparison shows the same paid-weeks flip deciding a $32-an-hour verdict.

When Your Hours Change Every Week

Most part-time schedules are not one fixed number. The method that holds up against a real schedule has three steps, and it deliberately refuses to annualize a single week:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Add the hours18 + 26 + 22 + 3096 hours over 4 weeks
Step 2 — Average the week96 ÷ 424.0 hours per week
Step 3 — Annualize the average$22 × 24 × 52$27,456.00 (if the pattern repeats)
Step 4 — Quote the actual too$22 × 96$2,112.00 for those 4 weeks, guaranteed

That “if the pattern repeats” qualifier is the whole point. A four-week window with a holiday rush in it annualizes to a year of holiday rushes; a quiet February annualizes to a year of quiet Februarys. Use at least four weeks, and a full quarter for seasonal work. Always put the measured period next to the annualized figure: “$27,456 annualized from a 96-hour four-week average” is honest in a way that “$27,456 a year” on its own is not. If your hours are truly unpredictable, budget on the lowest recent four-week average and treat anything above it as a bonus, not income.

What Lands in Your Bank Each Month

Annual figures are for comparing offers. Monthly figures are for paying rent. At $22 an hour and 24 hours a week, biweekly pay is $1,056 gross, and the calendar turns that into two kinds of month:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Two-paycheck month (gross)$1,056 × 2$2,112.00
Step 2 — Three-paycheck month (gross)$1,056 × 3$3,168.00
Step 3 — True monthly average (gross)$27,456 ÷ 12$2,288.00
Step 4 — True monthly average (take-home)$24,220.02 ÷ 12$2,018.34

Budget on the two-paycheck month, not the average. Ten months of the year carry two biweekly paychecks and two carry three, so a budget built on $2,288 will be $176 short in every two-check month. That is the same $176 the “times 4” shortcut hides. Treat the two three-paycheck months as windfalls: they are the year’s built-in savings, $1,056 gross each, not spending money. If you are paid semi-monthly instead, the problem goes away, 24 checks of $1,144, but so does the windfall, which is why semi-monthly workers rarely notice the biweekly trap. Check your own pay dates against your pay stub using our pay-stub guide.

Pro-Rata Salary: Reading a Salary Offer as a Part-Timer

Some part-time jobs quote a salary, not a rate, and the number on the offer is almost never the full-time salary. “$31,200 pro-rata” means the job pays 60% of a $52,000 full-time salary because it asks for 60% of full-time hours. The conversion runs the other way round from the rest of this guide:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Full-time hourly rate$52,000 ÷ 2,080 hours$25.00 per hour
Step 2 — Your share of full-time24 ÷ 40 hours60%
Step 3 — Pro-rata salary$52,000 × 60%$31,200.00 a year
Step 4 — Same figure, hourly route$25 × 24 × 52$31,200.00 a year
Step 5 — At 30 hours instead$52,000 × 75%$39,000.00 a year

Two checks before you accept a pro-rata figure. First, confirm the full-time base. A $31,200 offer is generous against a $52,000 full-time salary and thin against a $60,000 one, and the offer letter does not always print the base, so ask. Second, confirm the full-time hours: the same $52,000 salary is $25 an hour at a 40-hour week but $26.67 an hour at a 37.5-hour week, which changes every hourly comparison you make against it. And keep in mind what pro-rata does not scale on its own: paid time off and benefits may be prorated, capped, or left out entirely. That is a dollar question to settle before you sign, not after.

Overtime and Benefits: Two Part-Time Traps

The overtime trap. Federal overtime starts past 40 hours in a week, not past your scheduled hours. A 24-hour worker who adds an 8-hour Saturday works 32 hours, all at the straight $22 rate, $704 for the week. Counting that Saturday at time-and-a-half ($792) overstates the week by $88, and overstates a year of Saturdays by $4,576. The trap hits hardest when your “extra” shifts never push the week past 40: every extra hour is welcome, but none of it is premium pay unless a state daily-overtime rule or an employer policy says otherwise. Our double-time guide covers the rarer cases where 2× does apply.

The benefits line. Under the Affordable Care Act, large employers must offer affordable health coverage to employees averaging at least 30 hours a week (130 hours a month). That is why the 30-hour row of the ladder matters beyond its $34,320 gross and $29,756.12 take-home. At 29 hours, coverage is the employer’s choice; at 30, it is an obligation for large employers. That one hour can be worth more than its $1,144 of gross pay if it brings subsidized coverage with it, and it is a fair question to ask at offer stage: “At what weekly hours does health coverage start here?” Small employers are not bound by the same rule, so the answer varies, but the question never hurts.

After Taxes at Part-Time Hours (Federal Only)

Here is the after-tax sketch for the anchor schedule: single filer, 2026 rules, federal only, with state tax left out throughout:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Taxable income$27,456 − $16,100 standard deduction$11,356.00
Step 2 — Federal income tax10% × $11,356 (entirely in the 10% bracket)$1,135.60
Step 3 — FICA7.65% × $27,456 (6.2% Social Security + 1.45% Medicare)$2,100.38
Step 4 — Take-home$27,456 − $1,135.60 − $2,100.38$24,220.02 (88.2% kept)
Step 5 — Marginal rate10% federal + 7.65% FICA17.65% on the next dollar

Part-time keep-rates look generous for a simple reason: the standard deduction shelters the first $16,100 entirely, and at 24 hours the remaining $11,356 never leaves the 10% bracket. Compare a full-time $22-an-hour year ($45,760 gross, $38,948.16 take-home, 85.1% kept), where the 12% bracket takes a bigger bite. That generosity has a limit worth knowing. A $1 raise to $23 at 24 hours adds $1,248 gross but only $1,023.64 of take-home, because the raise pushes taxable income $204 past the $12,400 top of the 10% bracket, so part of it is taxed at 12%. Still a raise worth taking, just not a dollar-for-dollar one. Run your own filing status through the paycheck calculator before budgeting on these figures.

Nearby Rates at 24 Hours a Week

Same 24-hour schedule, different rates. This is the comparison a part-timer actually shops with. Take-home is federal-only, single filer, 2026 rules:

Hourly rateAnnual gross (24 hrs)Federal-only take-homeTake-home per monthLimitation
$18$22,464.00$20,109.10$1,675.76Lowest keep-rate cushion — small raises matter most here
$20$24,960.00$22,164.56$1,847.05Still entirely below the 12% bracket’s top
$22 (anchor)$27,456.00$24,220.02$2,018.34Raise to $23 crosses the 10% bracket’s top
$25$31,200.00$27,249.20$2,270.77Matches the $52,000 pro-rata example above
$30$37,440.00$32,263.04$2,688.59Approaches the 30-hour benefits-line income at 24 hours

Read the table as a negotiation tool. Moving from $20 to $22 at 24 hours is worth $2,055.46 of take-home a year ($171.29 a month), and moving from $22 to $25 is worth $3,029.18 ($252.43 a month). Hours beat rate only up to a point: adding 6 hours (24 to 30) at $22 is worth $5,536.10 of take-home, more than any single rate jump in the table. So when an employer cannot move on rate, ask about hours first.

Two Part-Time Jobs, One Annual Total

Two part-time jobs annualize by addition, not by averaging, and the combined figure can surprise you. Twenty hours at $20 an hour ($400 a week) plus 15 hours at $24 an hour ($360 a week) is $760 a week, or $39,520 a year gross. Federal-only take-home for a single filer on the combined $39,520 is $33,934.32 ($2,827.86 a month), the same take-home as a single $19-an-hour full-time job, because federal tax is worked out on total income, not per job. One practical warning: each employer withholds as if its job were your only income, so two jobs can under-withhold across the year even when each paycheck looks right. Check the combined figure on a paycheck calculator and fix your withholding early, not at tax time. Hours also stack for the overtime rule in a way people miss: 20 hours at one employer plus 25 at another is 45 hours of work but zero overtime hours, because the 40-hour rule applies per employer, not per worker.

How to Use the Calculator

Run your own schedule in four steps:

  1. Step 1 — Enter your rate and your real hours in the hourly-to-salary calculator. Use your averaged hours per week if they vary, not your best week.
  2. Step 2 — Set paid weeks honestly: 52 only if every week is paid. Drop to 50 or 48 for unpaid holidays, shutdowns, or school breaks.
  3. Step 3 — Check the monthly view against your two-paycheck months, and compare any salary offer with the salary-comparison calculator on the same paid-week basis.
  4. Step 4 — Run the paycheck calculator on the combined figure if you hold two jobs, so withholding reflects your total income rather than each job on its own.

Limitations

  1. Federal only: the after-tax sketch uses 2026 federal rules for a single filer on the standard deduction. State and local income taxes are left out, so your real take-home will be lower.
  2. Schedule assumptions: the figures use the schedule stated in each section. Different hours, paid-week counts, or seasonal patterns change every number, and variable hours annualize only if the pattern repeats.
  3. Overtime is per employer: the 40-hour federal threshold applies separately to each employer, and state daily-overtime rules or employer policies can differ from the federal default described here.
  4. Benefits vary by employer size and policy: the 30-hour ACA line binds large employers. Small employers, prorated benefits, and eligibility waiting periods can all change what a part-time offer is really worth.
  5. Salary comparisons exclude benefits: pro-rata figures are base pay only. Paid time off, a retirement match, or health coverage can outweigh a rate difference, so price them in dollars before deciding.
  6. Not tax or legal advice: the take-home sketch uses 2026 federal rules for a single filer on the standard deduction. Credits, other income, and filing status all change your real return.

Frequently Asked Questions

The questions we hear most about converting part-time hourly pay:

How do I convert part-time hourly pay to annual salary?

Take your hourly rate, multiply it by your hours per week, then multiply that by the number of paid weeks in the year: annual salary = rate × hours per week × paid weeks. At $22 an hour, 24 hours a week, and 52 paid weeks, that is $22 × 24 × 52 = $27,456 a year gross. The step most people skip is paid weeks. If two weeks a year are unpaid, use 50 weeks ($26,400), not 52. And if your hours vary, average them over a fair stretch first, then multiply.

How much is $22 an hour part-time at 24 hours a week?

Gross pay is $27,456 a year: $528 a week, $1,056 every two weeks, and $2,288 a month on average, before taxes. After federal income tax and FICA alone, a single filer on the 2026 standard deduction keeps $24,220.02 a year, which is $2,018.34 a month, or $931.54 per biweekly paycheck. State tax, retirement contributions, and health premiums aren't in that number, so a real paycheck will come in lower.

Should I use 52 weeks or 48 weeks for part-time annual pay?

Use the weeks you are actually paid for. Fifty-two weeks assumes every week of the year is paid, holidays and vacation included. If you are hourly and unpaid when you don't work, four unpaid weeks cut the same $22-an-hour, 24-hour schedule from $27,456 to $25,344 gross. That is a $2,112 difference, and $1,739.24 of take-home. The popular shortcut of multiplying a weekly figure by 4 to get a month quietly assumes a 48-week year, which is why it comes up $176 a month short on a fully paid schedule.

How do I calculate annual salary if my hours vary each week?

Average your weekly hours over a fair stretch, then annualize the average. Four recent weeks of 18, 26, 22, and 30 hours add up to 96 hours, an average of 24 a week. At $22 an hour that is $528 a week on average, or $27,456 if the pattern holds for 52 paid weeks. Don't annualize one busy week, and don't annualize a quiet one either: four weeks is the minimum window, and a full quarter is better for seasonal jobs. If the pattern won't repeat, say so, and quote the four-week actual ($2,112 here) next to the annualized figure.

What is a pro-rata salary and how do you calculate it?

A pro-rata salary is the share of a full-time salary that matches the share of full-time hours you work. Divide the full-time salary by full-time annual hours to get the hourly rate, then multiply by your hours. A $52,000 salary at 40 hours a week is $25 an hour ($52,000 ÷ 2,080). At 24 hours a week the pro-rata salary is $31,200 (60% of full-time), and at 30 hours it is $39,000 (75%). Federal-only take-home on $31,200 for a single filer is $27,249.20 a year.

Do part-time workers get overtime pay?

Only past 40 hours in a week, under federal law, the same rule as full-time workers. A part-timer who normally works 24 hours and picks up an extra 8-hour Saturday works a 32-hour week, all at the straight rate: $704 that week, not $792. That $88 gap is the overtime premium on hours that never crossed 40. Some states add daily-overtime rules, and some employers pay a premium by policy, but neither is the federal default. Check your state rules and your offer letter before counting on time-and-a-half.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

  • $22 an hour at 24 hours a week is $27,456 a year gross: $528 a week, $1,056 biweekly, $2,288 a month on average, and $24,220.02 kept after federal tax alone.
  • Paid weeks move the year by $2,112 gross: 52 paid weeks is $27,456, 48 paid weeks is $25,344, and the “times 4” month quietly assumes the 48-week year.
  • Variable hours annualize on the average: 18, 26, 22, and 30 hours average 24, and the $2,112 four-week actual is the only figure that is guaranteed.
  • Budget on two-paycheck months ($2,112 gross), not the $2,288 average, and treat the two three-paycheck months as savings.
  • A $52,000 salary is $31,200 pro-rata at 24 hours (60%) and $39,000 at 30 hours (75%). Always confirm the full-time base and full-time hours behind the quote.
  • Extra shifts are straight time until the week passes 40 hours: a 32-hour week pays $704, not $792. And 30 hours a week is the large-employer health-coverage line.
  • A $1 raise to $23 pays $1,023.64 more take-home at 24 hours, less than dollar-for-dollar, because part of the raise crosses into the 12% bracket.
  • Two jobs stack for income but not for overtime: $39,520 combined take-home is $33,934.32, yet 45 hours across two employers earns zero overtime hours.

Sources & Method

Gross figures use the stated schedule (rate × hours per week × paid weeks). Monthly averages divide the annual total by 12, and biweekly figures use 26 paychecks. The after-tax sketch uses 2026 federal rules for a single filer on the standard deduction: standard deduction $16,100, brackets 10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, 22% to $105,700 of taxable income, per IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32. FICA is 7.65% (Social Security 6.2% up to the $184,500 wage base, Medicare 1.45%), and all incomes here sit below the wage base. The 30-hour Affordable Care Act line reflects the large-employer shared-responsibility threshold of 30 hours a week on average (130 hours a month). State income tax, retirement contributions, health premiums, bonuses, and tips are left out except where a note says otherwise. This article is general information, not tax or legal advice.

3 Things to Remember

  1. The headline is $27,456 gross, $24,220.02 kept after federal tax alone, or $2,018.34 a month for a single filer at $22 an hour and 24 hours a week.
  2. Hours, paid weeks, and the monthly calendar move the year more than the rate itself: 30 hours is $34,320, four unpaid weeks cost $2,112, and two-paycheck months pay $2,112 gross against a $2,288 average.
  3. A pro-rata salary is a full-time salary scaled to your hours: $52,000 becomes $31,200 at 24 hours. And extra shifts stay at straight time until the week passes 40 hours.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.
  • Method: Full formulas, baselines, and rounding rules are on our calculation methodology page.
  • Coverage: U.S. federal rules; state and local rules vary and are not included.
  • Review: Last updated November 5, 2026.
  • Disclaimer: Estimates for planning only — not tax or legal advice.
